issues.legal_issue: The statutory exemption for an enlarged reserved area applies to a transfer or acquisition in that area only when the transaction is valid and bona fide.
material_facts: The land was included in an area added to land reserved for non-agricultural or industrial development.
The landlord’s son transferred the land during the period covered by the second proviso to Section 88(1)(b).
The son had no authority to manage or alienate the joint family property, and the transfer was found to be illegal and apparently intended to defeat the tenant’s statutory right.
issues.conclusion: The second proviso can apply to qualifying transfers or acquisitions in an added area, but only if they are valid and bona fide. The transfer in this case did not qualify, so the exemption did not displace the tenant’s statutory right.
issues.legal_principle: Section 88(1)(b) and its first proviso extend the exemption to an added area, with the provisions of Sections 1 to 87 treated as never having applied there. The second proviso treats a transfer or acquisition made within its specified interval as having occurred in an exempt area. The Court held that this treatment implicitly requires a valid, bona fide transaction, not one that is colourable, fraudulent, fictitious, or nominal. It considered Sukharam @ Bapusaheb Narayan Sanas v. Manikchand Motichand Shah, Mohanlal Chunilal Kothari v. Tribhovan Haribhai Tamboli, Sidram Narsappa Kamble v. Sholapur Borough Municipality, Parvati v. Fatehsinhrao Pratapsinhrao Gaekwad, and Navinchandra Ramanlal v. Kalidas Bhudarbai; the Court noted that Navinchandra did not consider the second proviso’s effect.

rule.if: added_area_exemption_dispute and transfer_or_acquisition_within_statutory_window and transaction_genuine and transferor_had_authority

predicates.added_area_exemption_dispute: The case concerns whether a statutory tenancy exemption extends to land added to an area reserved for non-agricultural or industrial development.
predicates.transfer_or_acquisition_within_statutory: A person transferred or acquired the land during the interval covered by the special rule for transactions in an added area.
predicates.transaction_genuine: The transfer or acquisition was not colourable, fraudulent, fictitious, or nominal.
predicates.transferor_had_authority: The person who transferred the land had authority to make that transfer.

issues.definition: When an exemption dispute concerns added land and a transaction within the applicable interval, the land is exempt from tenancy protections if the transaction was genuine and made by an authorized transferor.

issues.legal_issue: A junior member cannot alienate joint family property as manager while the senior manager remains alive and has not relinquished management, unless an exceptional circumstance or a competent court appointment authorizes the junior member to act.
material_facts: A tenant had acquired a statutory deemed-purchaser interest in agricultural land, although exercise of the purchase right was deferred because the landlord was under a disability.
The landlord, who was the joint family’s senior manager, was alive when his son sold the land to a third party.
The son had not been appointed manager by a competent court under the Lunacy Act, and no exceptional family circumstance authorizing him to act was present.
The tenant relied on the son’s lack of authority to argue that the sale could not defeat the tenant’s statutory right.
issues.conclusion: The son’s sale was illegal and did not bind the tenant. Because the sale was not a valid and bona fide transaction, the second proviso did not apply, and the tenant’s deemed-purchaser right survived the later notification.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 32(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, the tenant acquired a deemed-purchaser right; Section 32-F deferred exercise of the purchase right because of the landlord’s disability. Section 88(1)(b), including its second proviso, could not protect an unauthorized sale from defeating that right. Under Hindu joint family law, management belongs to the senior manager, and a junior member cannot act as manager while that manager is available unless management was relinquished or exceptional circumstances justified the junior member’s action. Where the senior manager was incapacitated, the Court held that a competent court appointment under Sections 39, 43, and 45 of the Indian Lunacy Act was required. The Court relied on P.K. Gobindan Nair v. P. Narayanan Nair and A. Ramacharlu v. Archakan Ananthacharlu.

rule.if: tenant_statutory_purchase_right_dispute and tenant_had_statutory_purchase_interest and senior_family_manager_alive and junior_member_sold_family_property and not competent_court_appointed_junior_manager and not exceptional_circumstances_authorized_sale

predicates.tenant_statutory_purchase_right_dispute: The proceeding concerns whether a sale of leased agricultural land defeats a tenant’s statutory purchase interest.
predicates.tenant_had_statutory_purchase_interest: The tenant had acquired a statutory interest in purchasing the land, even if exercise of the purchase right was deferred.
predicates.senior_family_manager_alive: The senior manager of the joint family was alive when the sale occurred.
predicates.junior_member_sold_family_property: A junior member of the joint family sold property belonging to the family.
predicates.competent_court_appointed_junior_manager: A competent court appointed the junior member to manage the family property.
predicates.exceptional_circumstances_authorized_sal: The senior manager had relinquished management or exceptional circumstances justified the junior member’s sale.

issues.definition: A tenant’s statutory purchase interest survives when a junior family member sells family property while the senior manager is alive and neither a competent court appointment nor an exceptional circumstance authorized the junior member to act.
